analysis.one_liner: Requires a background check for every private firearm sale, run through a licensed dealer.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2025 with 46 cosponsors — every Senate Democrat and Independent — and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for one private person to sell or give a firearm to another unless a licensed gun dealer first takes possession and runs a background check, the same check that already applies to sales at gun stores. It exempts gifts within families, loans at shooting ranges, hunting, and transfers made in self-defense emergencies. It has not moved since it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially in communities affected by gun violence. Private sales, gun shows, and online sales are the main channels that let people who are legally barred from owning guns — convicted felons, domestic abusers — buy them with no questions asked. Routing every transfer through a licensed dealer closes that gap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for an unlicensed person to transfer a firearm to another unlicensed person unless a licensed dealer, manufacturer, or importer first takes possession to run the standard background check required of gun stores [S2] [S3].
Licensed dealers handling a private transfer must follow all the same rules as a regular store sale, so the buyer is checked against federal prohibition records the same way [S3].
The bill leaves state laws untouched and states it may not be used to build a national gun registry [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private gun sellers and buyers. Every private sale would require a trip to a licensed dealer and typically a transfer fee, and informal transfers not covered by the family, hunting, range, or emergency exemptions would become federal crimes. Licensed dealers, by contrast, gain a stream of new fee-paying transfer business.

drawbacks.text: Buyers would pay dealer transfer fees on every private sale, a real cost for people trading or selling used guns [S2].

The exemption list is detailed but not infinite; some lawful arrangements — lending a gun to a friend for a trip, certain family handoffs outside the listed relationships — would require a dealer visit or become illegal, and otherwise-lawful owners bear the burden of knowing the rules [S3].

Opponents of universal checks argue that people already banned from buying guns will still obtain them illegally, so the requirement chiefly burdens law-abiding sellers and buyers. That objection is a policy argument, not a claim about the bill's text [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is potentially large: background checks are the standard tool for keeping guns away from people with felony or domestic violence records, and private sales are the main hole in that system. The costs are real but modest — transfer fees and paperwork for lawful owners, plus some complexity in the exemption rules. The serious honest objection is enforcement: a federal requirement only deters sellers willing to follow the law, and illegal sellers may keep operating underground. On balance the bill is a straightforward, if partial, safety measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on November 19, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S5].
46 senators cosponsored it — 44 of the 45 Senate Democrats and both Independents [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the committee referral: no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, no one has lost anything, because nothing has changed: private gun transfers remain check-free, and the Senate majority has not had to take a position on the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the status quo holds

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut, bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Background Check Expansion Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on November 19, 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: 55 Senate Republicans; sets the Senate calendar and committee agendas
against.what_they_did: No Republican has cosponsored the bill, and the majority has not scheduled any action on it.

against.name: National Rifle Association and gun-rights groups
against.role: Outside advocacy organizations opposing universal background checks
against.what_they_did: Longstanding, publicly stated opposition to expanding background checks to private sales, pressuring senators to oppose such bills.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat or Independent — 44 of 45 Senate Democrats and both Independents — with no Republican cosponsor in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats.

industries.note: The bill makes licensed dealers the mandatory middleman for every private firearm transfer, guaranteeing them a stream of transfer business. Buyers pay the dealer a fee and give up some convenience, though the policy's purpose — keeping guns from prohibited buyers — is a public-safety goal the dealers' role now serves.

industries.industry: Unlicensed private sellers and gun-show and online sellers
industries.note: These sellers lose the ability to complete a sale with no check and no third party. Their interest in an unrestricted market runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.

analysis.trajectory: With a 55-seat Republican majority, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since referral, the realistic path is that the bill dies in the Judiciary Committee and never reaches a floor vote before this Congress ends in January 2027.
